content: Infectious waste includes materials such as laboratory cultures, microbiological stocks, and waste containing excreta or other substances that have come into contact with patients suffering from highly infectious diseases in isolation wards. Bain and Johnston, in their 2018 study published in the Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development, explored data gaps and opportunities for national monitoring of institutional WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Their scoping study, which covered 10 countries across Latin America, the Caribbean, and East Asia-Pacific regions, identified 14 national data sources for WASH in healthcare facilities (HCFs). To monitor WASH in HCFs, service ladders similar to those used for household WASH and WASH in schools were proposed. These multi-level service ladders enable countries at varying stages of development to progressively meet SDG criteria and track their progress. Separate ladders are defined for each indicator, with core service levels categorized as no service, limited service, and basic service. For countries where basic service is not sufficiently ambitious, an advanced service level can be defined, allowing nations to establish their own criteria based on their context and facility type. Annex A provides a menu of options for countries to expand upon the core question set when basic services are insufficient or when national or sub-national priorities extend beyond the basic criteria. Basic Service Requirements: 1. Hand Hygiene: Functional hand hygiene facilities (with water and soap and/or alcohol-based hand rub) must be available at points of care and within 5 meters of toilets. 2. Cleaning Protocols: Basic cleaning protocols must be in place, and all staff responsible for cleaning must receive training. 3. Limited Service: Hand hygiene facilities may be available at either points of care or toilets, but not both. There may be limited separation, treatment, or disposal of sharps and infectious waste, and cleaning protocols may exist, but not all staff may be trained. 4. No Service: No cleaning protocols are available, and no staff have received cleaning training. Core WASH Questions for HCF Surveys: The core questions are the minimum required to report on SDG indicators. These questions are divided into five sections: water, sanitation, hygiene, healthcare waste management, and environmental cleaning. Water Supply: The main water supply for the facility should be identified, including its type and location (e.g., on-premises or within 500 meters). The availability of water at the time of the survey is also assessed. A reliable water supply is critical for infection prevention and control, as well as for general facility operations. Sanitation: Questions assess the type and usability of toilets, their availability for staff and patients, and whether they are sex-separated or gender-neutral. Toilets must also accommodate menstrual hygiene needs and be accessible to individuals with limited mobility. Hygiene: Hand hygiene is essential for infection prevention. Functional hand hygiene facilities must be available at points of care and near toilets. These facilities should include soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR), though ABHR alone is insufficient for removing fecal matter. Healthcare Waste Management: Proper segregation of waste into at least three labeled bins (sharps, infectious, and non-infectious waste) is required. Waste treatment and disposal methods, such as autoclaving, incineration, or burial in a lined, protected pit, must meet basic service standards. Environmental Cleaning: Cleaning protocols should include step-by-step techniques for specific tasks and a cleaning schedule specifying responsibilities and frequency. All staff responsible for cleaning must receive structured training. Data Analysis and Reporting: Guidance is provided for calculating WASH service levels in HCFs based on survey responses. Indicators include the proportion of facilities with improved water supplies, usable and accessible toilets, hand hygiene facilities, and safe waste management practices. These calculations help monitor progress toward achieving SDG targets and identify disparities at national and sub-national levels. In summary, the effective functioning of healthcare facilities relies on safe and reliable WASH services. These services are critical for infection prevention, patient dignity, and the overall quality of care.
